concepts.title: Shepherd Ajamil and the Starving Tigers
concepts.definition: Arun Kolatkar retells a folk fable in free verse: tigers, starving, complain to their king that shepherd Ajamil's dogs guard the sheep too well and they have had nothing to eat. The tiger king sends word to Ajamil, summoning the shepherd to a parley he may not refuse.
concepts.key_idea: A fable reborn in free verse -- hungry tigers, guarded sheep, and a summons no shepherd can refuse.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww122.txt opening sections (tiger people complain to their king, starving, nothing to eat, ajamil's dogs guarding sheep, summons to the shepherd)

solution_steps.explain: The tigers protest their starvation -- Ajamil's loyal dogs make his flock unraidable.
Their king dispatches an invitation -- the polite form of a threat.
Ajamil must answer the tiger court: sheep, dogs and wits against royal appetite.

concepts.title: The Parley and Ajamil's Cunning Peace
concepts.definition: At the meeting Ajamil uses not weapons but wine and flattery: he gets the tiger king and his court drunk on home-brew, praises their magnificence, and brokers a treaty -- the tigers will never hunt his flock again if he supplies them regularly with a sheep or goat, delivered to their door without slaughter or pursuit.
concepts.key_idea: No sword, only wine and wit -- the shepherd turns a predator's court into a treaty table.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww122.txt parley sections (home brew, flattery of the tiger king, the treaty, sheep or goat delivered regularly, no hunting of the flock)

solution_steps.explain: Ajamil arrives with liquor, and toasts loosen the tiger court's menace into cheer.
Flattering their majesty, he proposes a compact -- regular tribute of one animal for total peace.
The drunk court agrees; the treaty ends predation on the flock by making the shepherd the supplier.

concepts.title: The Wolf's Slander and the Shepherd's Answer
concepts.definition: A jealous wolf spreads slander that Ajamil cheats the tigers. The tiger king summons the old shepherd once more; Ajamil offers to explain, then simply keeps sending the promised animals on time -- and the slander dies of starvation, with no counter-argument needed. Kolatkar's moral glints: a kept promise outlives any malicious tongue.
concepts.key_idea: The best answer to slander is a delivery made on time -- promises kept silence even a tiger court.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww122.txt slander sections (jealous wolf, slander against ajamil, second summons, deliveries continue on time, slander dies, moral of the poem)

solution_steps.explain: The wolf whispers that Ajamil shortchanges the tigers -- the treaty, it claims, is a fraud.
Summoned again, Ajamil says the deliveries will speak for him and keeps sending the animals punctually.
With nothing to feed on, the wolf's lie starves -- Kolatkar's fable closes on integrity proved by habit.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Describe how Ajamil prepares for and conducts his meeting with the tiger king.

solution_template.explain: He brings no weapons -- only a skin of home-brew and a ready tongue.
He drinks the court merry and seasons it with compliments on its majesty.
A treaty is signed: one animal delivered regularly in exchange for the flock's total safety.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does Ajamil refuse to argue against the wolf's slander before the tiger king?

solution_template.explain: Words against words would only give the lie a stage.
Ajamil lets the uninterrupted deliveries answer -- fact as the only plea.
The slander starves for lack of evidence -- Kolatkar's witty proof that kept promises silence malice.
